findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` using the raw email string passed in from the validator (which in turn comes from `user.email`, which is never normalized/downcased before this check). Since the comparison is a case-sensitive SQL match (and the unique index on `blocked_emails.email` is also case sensitive), an email that was blocked as `bad@spammers.org` can be bypassed simply by registering as `Bad@Spammers.org` or `BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG`. This defeats the entire purpose of the blocked-email feature.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write race condition on match_count/last_match_at
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the record, increments `match_count` in Ruby, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `save`. Under concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email, two requests can both read the same `match_count`, increment it independently, and save, causing lost updates (the counter under-reports actual match attempts). This should use an atomic update (e.g. `update_counters`/`UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`) instead of load-then-save.

findings.title: should_block? side-effects run multiple times per signup attempt, inflating match_count
findings.body: `should_block?` is called from the `email` EachValidator, which runs every time `valid?`/`save` triggers validations. In `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb), `user.valid?` is called once (to decide whether to call DiscourseHub), and then `user.save` triggers validations again internally. This means a single signup attempt against a blocked email can increment `match_count` by 2 (or more, if other code paths call `valid?`), making the recorded match statistics inaccurate and misleading for any analysis or reporting based on `match_count`/`last_match_at`.

findings.title: Account-creation failure response now leaks raw validation errors and submitted email
findings.body: The `create` action's failure branch now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to the client. This echoes back the submitted email (even when rejected for being blocked, already taken, or disallowed by whitelist/blacklist) along with the specific validation error keys. This allows an attacker to probe arbitrary email addresses and learn whether they are already registered, blocked, or restricted by domain policy without ever creating an account — a user/email-enumeration vector that did not exist before (previously only a combined message string was exposed).

findings.title: No test coverage for whitelist/blacklist branches moved out of User model
findings.body: `app/models/user.rb` previously had `email_validator`/`email_in_restriction_setting?` methods handling `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` and `email_domains_blacklist`, and this logic has been moved into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. The new spec file only tests the `BlockedEmail` branch (lines 9-21); it does not exercise the whitelist or blacklist branches (lines 4-12 of email_validator.rb) at all, so a regression in that moved logic (e.g. regex construction, which setting takes precedence) would go undetected. Any prior tests for this logic that existed against `User` should be confirmed as migrated here, otherwise this behavior now has no automated coverage.

findings.title: Validator always invokes should_block? even with no record errors check limited to one attribute, could run against blank/invalid values
findings.body: `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` whenever the whitelist/blacklist checks pass, without guarding against `value` being blank or malformed. Although presence is validated elsewhere on `User`, this validator can be reused on other models/attributes where blank or nil values might reach `should_block?`, causing an unnecessary `BlockedEmail.where(email: nil)` query and wasted BlockedEmail record lookups. A `return if value.blank?` guard would make this validator more robust and reusable.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array literal shared at prototype definition time
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined directly on the controller's prototype as a shared array literal rather than being created fresh per instance (e.g. in an `init` hook). If more than one instance of `CreateAccountController` is ever created (tests, multiple modal opens without a full page reload, etc.), all instances share and mutate the same array, so rejected emails from one session/instance can leak into another, causing emails to be incorrectly reported as previously rejected.
